passage:
Madhav's diary, Thursday night.
Day 9 at the architects' office. Today Mr Sood, the partner, barked, “Who taught you to staple?” in front of eight people, and nobody looked up. Then I photocopied drawings for six hours. I keep wondering whether this is just how it is. I wanted to apologise to everyone, even for breathing. At tea, Afreen didi, the senior architect, sat next to me. She said, “Copying and stapling is what interns do first. But being barked at in front of the team isn't something you should have to swallow. You can ask, 'Could you tell me privately how you want it?' If it keeps happening, tell the intern coordinator and me.” My hands are still a bit shaky. Tomorrow I'll try the sentence.
Madhav

qa.q: How many people were in the room when Mr Sood barked at Madhav?
qa.a: Eight people were there when Mr Sood barked.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling after the shouting and the six hours of copying?
qa.a: Madhav felt small and unsure whether this was normal, wanting to apologise to everyone even for breathing, and still had shaky hands.

qa.q: What did Afreen say that helped Madhav tell normal from unfair?
qa.a: Afreen said that copying and stapling is what interns do first, but being barked at in front of the team is not something to swallow, and gave a sentence to use and a place to go if it continues.

qa.q: Why might the eight people in the room have kept their eyes down?
qa.a: They may have been unsure how to step in or fearful of the partner, which fits nobody looking up and shows how a rigid hierarchy keeps people quiet.

grounding: An intern is spoken to sharply and given menial work and a mentor helps tell what is normal from what is unfair.

passage:
Harish: bhaiya are you free? rough week at the newspaper office
Bhupen: Tell me.
Harish: the news editor threw a file on my desk and said “my tea, not this rubbish” in front of the whole desk. everyone just kept typing
Bhupen: What had you done?
Harish: fetched tea four times today, then wrote three city briefs, then he said the briefs were rubbish
Bhupen: Tea runs and briefs are normal for an intern. Being shouted at in front of everyone isn't. Did any of the feedback on the briefs concern the actual work?
Harish: he said the second para was buried
Bhupen: That part is useful. The shouting isn't. Ask him next time for feedback in private, and if it repeats, talk to the internship coordinator. I'll come with you if you want.
Harish: ok. I'll feel small tomorrow but I'll try
Bhupen: You're not small. Call me after.

qa.q: How many times had Harish fetched tea that day?
qa.a: Harish had fetched tea four times that day.

qa.q: Why did Harish say, “I'll feel small tomorrow but I'll try”?
qa.a: Harish still feels small after being shouted at in front of the whole desk, yet is willing to try Bhupen's suggestions.

qa.q: What did Bhupen suggest for handling the editor's feedback in future?
qa.a: Bhupen suggested asking the editor for feedback in private and, if the shouting repeats, talking to the internship coordinator, with Bhupen offering to go along.

qa.q: What might Bhupen be thinking when he says, “You're not small”?
qa.a: Bhupen seems to want Harish to stop believing the shouting says something about Harish's worth, and wants to stay close for support.

grounding: An intern is shouted at and given menial work, and a trusted mentor helps the intern tell normal tasks from unfair treatment.
